A working tool: load an image of a relief (a render, a photo, or a sheet with several views) and get a smooth, watertight 3D model sized for CNC relief carving, with a 3D viewer, toolpath preview and STL, OBJ, heightmap and outline exports. 06How the Model Is BuiltMETHOD▶

The same pipeline as the smooth Jelinek Family sign STL, rebuilt to run in the browser. What keeps the result smooth instead of stepped: float heights end to end (no 8-bit terracing), a blend of blurs instead of raw brightness, smooth resampling, and a fine grid.

#TopicStep
1Find viewsIn a composite sheet, separate shapes are grouped into views; thin frame rectangles and small label text are ignored. The first large view is the front.
2SilhouetteBackground colour is read from the crop border. Pixels that differ enough become the sign; the largest connected piece is kept, holes are filled, and a small opening removes whiskers.
3ResampleThe sign’s bounding box is resampled with high-quality (bicubic-style) smoothing to the grid: sign width ÷ grid spacing points across.
4HeightBrightness (or a chosen channel) becomes raw height, kept in 32-bit float. Optional lighting correction subtracts a wide blur.
5BlendThree Gaussian-blurred copies — broad, medium and fine — are blended by weight: a weighted band-pass that gives big shapes smooth slopes.
6NormalizeHeights inside the sign are mapped from the low to the high percentile onto 0–1, then gamma and terraces are applied.
7Roll-offA Euclidean distance transform from the outline rounds the edge with a sine shoulder down to the slab.
8Tool reachA drop-cutter pass with the finishing ball, then the ball’s envelope, gives what the tool can actually leave; the difference is the Tool reach map, or it replaces the model.
HHeightmap modeFor a grayscale heightmap, steps 2–6 are replaced: the PNG is decoded exactly (all 65,536 levels of a 16-bit file, not the browser’s 8-bit copy), resampled bicubically, cut out where it is black, lightly smoothed only to remove 8-bit steps, and mapped linearly from the black and white levels to slab and full depth.
9MeshThe viewer and exports use the same grid: two triangles (or one quad) per cell inside the outline, a flat bottom, and walls along every outline edge — a closed, watertight solid.
Shading is not depthHeight comes from how light falls on the image, a heuristic and not a true 3D reconstruction. Bright paint reads as high and cast shadows read as low. The settings let you steer it, and the viewer shows the result before you cut.

  • Vectric Aspire / VCarveImport the STL as a component (Model › Import Component / 3D Model), or the 16-bit heightmap as a bitmap component. Import the outline SVG for the profile cut.
  • CarvecoImport the STL or the 16-bit PNG as a relief, set the size in millimetres, then add the outline vectors.

08Getting a Good Source ImageGUIDANCE▶

The page takes two kinds of image, and they work very differently. A true heightmap stores height directly: each gray value is a depth, so the model comes out exactly as drawn. A shaded image (a render, photo or drawing) only shows how light falls on a shape, so the page has to guess the height, and shadows, paint and highlights can fool it. Use a heightmap whenever you can find or make one.

TopicTrue heightmapShaded image
What it showsHeight as gray: black is the lowest point (or cut away), white is the highestLight and shadow on a surface, as a camera or renderer sees it
How it looksSoft and flat-looking, with no light direction, no cast shadows and no shineLooks 3D: one side of each shape is lit and the other side is dark
Where it comes fromRelief or CAM software (Vectric Aspire, Carveco), a 3D program’s depth or displacement pass, depth-map AI tools, or this page’s own Heightmap exportAI image generators, 3D renders, photos of carvings, drawings
What the page doesReads the gray exactly (all 65,536 levels of a 16-bit PNG) and maps black and white to the slab and full relief depthEstimates height from brightness with a blend of blurs: a best guess, not a measurement
AccuracyExact: what you see is what you carveApproximate: check it in 3D Model Viewer and tune the Height settings
Best file16-bit grayscale PNG; 8-bit works with light de-step smoothingPNG or a good-quality JPG, about 1000 px across or more
Image is settinga heightmap (gray = height)a render or photo (shading)

Which kind do I have? Five quick checks:

  • Light directionIf one side of every letter or shape is bright and the other side dark, the image is shaded. A heightmap looks the same from every side.
  • Flat topsOn a heightmap, a flat raised area is one even gray. On a shaded image its brightness changes with the light.
  • ColourHeightmaps are grayscale. Colour means a shaded image or paint. A purple and blue normal map is not a heightmap and won’t work here.
  • File nameNames with height, depth, displacement or bump are usually heightmaps; auto-detect looks for them.
  • Quick testSet Image is to heightmap. If the model comes out tilted, with every shape sloping toward one side, the image is shaded.

Getting a good heightmap:

  • 16-bit if you canAn 8-bit map has only 256 levels, which can show as steps on a deep relief. De-step smoothing hides most of them.
  • Black outsidePure black around the part becomes cut-out (the Cut-out below setting), so the outline comes from the map itself.
  • Full rangeBlack to white gives the full relief depth. If the map uses only part of the range, turn on Stretch to full depth.
  • Set the depthA heightmap has no units. Set Relief depth to the depth it was made for. Maps exported from this page remember their size and Z range.
  • No baked lightA gray render with shadows or ambient occlusion is still a shaded image, even if it looks gray.

If you only have a shaded image, the model can only be as good as the brightness in it. The best ones look like a sculpted relief already.

  • Even greyA single material colour (grey, clay, bone) with no painted colours: brightness then means shape, not paint.
  • Soft lightLight from the front or slightly above, with no hard cast shadows. Shadows read as holes.
  • Plain backgroundBlack, white or transparent behind the sign, so the outline separates cleanly.
  • Straight onThe front view square to the camera; a perspective photo makes the model lean.
  • ResolutionAt least as many pixels across as grid points (about 1000 for a 610 mm sign at 0.6 mm).
  • Multi-view sheetsFront, top, right and isometric panels on black, like the sample. The top and right views let the page estimate the thickness.
Prompt idea for an AI image“Orthographic front view of a carved wooden relief sign, uniform light grey clay material, soft frontal lighting, no cast shadows, pure black background, high detail, no perspective.” Add the text and motifs you want.
09Limitations and CautionsGUIDANCE▶
  • Depth accuracyHeight is estimated from shading, not measured. Undercuts and hidden sides can’t be recovered from a front view.
  • Painted colourDark paint on a raised letter makes it low. Use invert, a single channel, or a grey render.
  • Outline stepsThe outline follows the grid, a staircase as fine as the grid spacing. The exported outline splines are smoothed; use them for the profile cut.
  • Browser memoryGrids are capped near 2.2 million points. Very large signs get a coarser grid automatically; exports at full detail can be tens of megabytes.
  • Graphics resetsThe browser can take the 3D view’s graphics away (low graphics memory, many 3D tabs, a graphics switch or driver reset). The viewer rebuilds itself in a couple of seconds and keeps a log in 3D health; after three resets in two minutes it stops and offers the basic viewer.
  • Toolpath previewThe preview is a cutting simulation for timing and reach, not G-code. Program the real toolpaths in your CAM software.
  • RightsUse images you own or have permission to carve.

TermTopicDefinitionAppears inQty
HeightmapHeightA grid or grayscale image where each value is a height.
ReliefHeightA carving raised from a flat background, viewed from the front.
Front viewImagesThe straight-on view of the sign; it alone builds the model.
Multi-view sheetImagesOne image holding several views of an object, such as front, top, right and isometric.
SilhouetteImagesThe outline of the sign separated from its background.
Bicubic resamplingImagesResizing that fits smooth curves between pixels, so slopes stay continuous.
Gaussian blurHeightA smoothing filter that averages each point with its neighbours by a bell curve; σ is its width.
Band-passHeightWeighting some feature sizes over others; here, broad shapes over fine noise.
PercentileHeightThe value below which a given share of the points fall; used to ignore a few extreme highlights.
GammaHeightA curve applied to heights: above 1 deepens the mid-tones, below 1 lifts them.
TerracesHeightFlat height levels, either wanted (2.5D carving) or an artifact of too few levels.
Edge roll-offMeshThe rounded shoulder where the relief meets the slab at the outline.
Distance transformMeshFor each point, its distance to the nearest outline point.
WatertightMeshA closed mesh with no gaps, so it encloses a solid.
STLFilesA triangle mesh file, the common input for CAM and 3D printing.
OBJFilesA mesh file that can hold quads and texture coordinates.
16-bit PNGFilesA grayscale image with 65,536 levels, used as a heightmap by relief software.
DXF / SVGFilesVector formats for 2D curves, used for the profile cut outline and contours.
Ball-noseCuttingA cutter with a rounded tip, used for 3D finishing; a tapered ball has a cone above the tip.
StepoverCuttingSideways distance between finishing passes; smaller leaves smaller ridges.
Scallop / cuspCuttingThe small ridge a ball leaves between two passes.
Drop-cutterCuttingLowering the cutter at each point until it touches the surface, giving the tool tip height.
Tool reachCuttingWhere a given ball can reach the surface; tighter spots keep extra material.
Profile cutCuttingA 2D cut along the outline that frees the part from the stock, usually with tabs.
StockCuttingThe raw board the sign is carved from.
Parallel toolpathCuttingStraight back-and-forth passes across the part, the usual relief finish.
OrthographicViewerA view with no perspective, so sizes don’t shrink with distance.
View cubeViewerThe small cube in the viewer’s corner that shows and sets the view direction.
Section cutViewerTrimming the model from a side to see its profile.
Shape from shadingHeightEstimating height from how light falls on the image.
